intro_html:
HB 1129 has not moved since April 2026, and unless lawmakers adopt a new adjournment resolution it cannot be taken up before the 2025–26 General Assembly ends; a new bill would have to be filed when the legislature convenes in January 2027. In Charlotte the utility is Duke Energy Carolinas, and North Carolina’s statewide interconnection procedures route even a certified inverter-based system of 20 kW or less through an interconnection request and a certificate of completion. Until the utility’s witness test is done or waived, the owner “has no right to operate in parallel” with the grid.

The state’s solar-access statute, G.S. 22B-20, voids covenants that would prohibit solar collectors on “residential property”, but that term excludes any condominium “located in a multi-story building” whose units have horizontal boundaries — stacked flats, in other words. Even where the statute applies, it lets a covenant bar collectors visible from the ground on a facade facing a street or common area, which can include a front balcony. A condo owner in a Charlotte tower, like a renter, needs permission.

At North Carolina’s average price of 14.6¢, well below the US average of 17.9¢, payback is long, so the details of a particular balcony matter; balco.nyc’s calculator models a specific Charlotte address with the rate from your own bill.

faq: Does North Carolina's solar access law protect condo balconies?

No. G.S. 22B-20 voids covenants that would prohibit solar collectors on residential property, but it excludes condominiums in multi-story buildings whose units have horizontal boundaries, and it still allows covenants barring collectors visible from the ground on a facade facing a street or common area.
